short: The day the Swedish field army was destroyed and Russia became a great power.
full:
Charles XII had invaded Russia in 1708, lost his supply and reinforcement column when Lewenhaupt's convoy was cut up at Lesnaya, and wintered in Ukraine through the coldest European winter in centuries. By the summer of 1709 he was besieging Poltava with perhaps 24,000 men, short of powder and with most of his guns silent. He was shot through the foot days before the battle and had to be carried in a litter, leaving command to Rehnskiöld.

The Swedish attack on 8 July went in against entrenched redoubts before dawn and lost cohesion; a column under Roos was cut off and forced to surrender. When the main Russian line of some 40,000 came out of its camp behind heavy artillery, the Swedish infantry broke. Charles escaped south into Ottoman territory with about 1,500 men, while roughly 20,000 survivors surrendered at Perevolochna three days later. Sweden never fielded an army of that quality again. Sabaton's "Poltava" takes the defeat as its subject.
